prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing frequency standards to a new regime of accuracy

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part B005 prize for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye and have not changed my configuration since round 1; what has changed is that the chair's questions let me state the deciding criterion explicitly. The criterion I would apply is: a prize should reward a discovery or invention whose central claim is settled independently of interpretation, whose originality is separable from earlier prizes, and whose credit can be assigned within three names without a visible injustice inside the credited set. B005 meets all three. The invention is a single idea, trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength so the lattice light shift cancels for the clock transition, which is what turned a statistical advantage into a systematic-limited clock at about 1e-18. That performance has been reproduced and surpassed with several species in laboratories in Japan, the United States and Europe, and international clock comparisons are now routine, so the result does not depend on one group or on a theoretical reading. On exact credit, I take Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice spectroscopy and Ye for carrying the clock to record accuracy and stability; I treat the Tokyo-Boulder priority detail as recollection that the committee should verify, and I would word the citation so that it is correct under either reading of fine priority. On distinctness from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, the magic-wavelength lattice is not in either citation, so I regard this as a different invention in the same broad territory, not a second prize for the same lineage.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain after round 1 are real. First, this is precision-measurement science adjacent to two earlier prizes, and Mehlig's question whether a clock is a discovery about nature or an instrument achievement has no clean answer; I think the invention criterion covers it, but a committee that weights new phenomena above new instruments would reasonably prefer B014. Second, the pending redefinition of the second is a prospective application, and I do not want to argue that it validates the case. Third, a two-name credit omits other lattice-clock groups (Paris, PTB and others), ultrastable-laser developers and ion-clock groups reaching comparable accuracy by a different route, and I cannot settle from the supplied material how much of the 1e-18 result belongs to them. Finally, B014 has the widest opening ranking (all eight members, highest Borda total), so a decision for B005 is a decision for tighter attribution and a longer record over breadth of community impact, and I should say so openly.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B014 first on the discovery itself, argues the correlated states are stable regardless of the superconducting mechanism, and sees no reason the case will improve by waiting.
responses.response: I accept the first two points. The correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle are reproduced widely, and a citation limited to flat bands and observed states does not depend on the pairing mechanism, so I do not treat the open mechanism as disqualifying. Where I still differ is on credit rather than science. Your own file concedes that Yuan Cao and the earlier twisted-bilayer band theorists fall outside the trio, and you rest the experimental seat on the convention that the group leader is credited. That is a defensible convention, but it means the committee would knowingly make an incomplete allocation, whereas for B005 the omissions lie outside the credited pair and do not split the discovery itself. On urgency, I do not think a fast-moving field argues for acting now: if the picture is stable, waiting costs little, and the redefinition of the second does not make the lattice-clock case less ready today. I would not resist B014 if the committee decides eight years is enough, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig frames the choice as a new-phenomenon prize (B014) versus a measurement-science prize (B005) and asks whether a clock is a discovery about nature or an instrument achievement.
responses.response: I think the question is a fair one and I do not claim it has a decisive answer. My view is that the criterion should be what the work changed about what can be measured and tested, not whether nature surprised us. Magic-wavelength trapping changed the accessible regime of fractional uncertainty by about two orders of magnitude and made tests of constants and relativistic geodesy routine, and it did so with an instrument that has been independently rebuilt many times. That is an invention in the sense the criterion intends. I also agree with you that the citation wording matters here: it should name the lattice clock and not precision timekeeping in general, so it cannot be read as a third prize for the comb and ion-control lineage. I recognise that you move to B014 on maturity of the prediction-plus-confirmation structure, and I do not think that structure is wrong, only that it is younger and its credit is less clean.

responses.point: Kroll holds B005 first, considers the attribution the cleanest on the shortlist, and flags that B014 has broader opening support and that the IceCube case rests on a single collaboration with partial source identification.
responses.response: I agree that B014 draws wider support and that this should be recorded rather than denied. I also accept your point on B035, and it moves me: the diffuse astrophysical flux is a real discovery, but it is collaboration-scale, the pioneer chain from DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA makes any three-name cut arbitrary (including my own two-name proposal), and source identification is incomplete. I therefore keep B035 only as a later-year alternative and not as a competitor to B005 in this round. On B005, I would ask us to be careful about your phrase 'cleanest attribution': it is clean within the pair, but your own recollection of Hall's laboratory is a reminder that the Boulder-Tokyo priority record deserves a source check before the vote, and I would keep the citation worded so that it does not assert more about priority than the committee has verified.

responses.point: Johansson argues that a pending redefinition of the second is a use of the invention and not a condition of its validity, and that the clock credit is cleaner than the B014 theory attribution.
responses.response: I agree with the first point and have adjusted my own round-1 wording: I listed the unrealized redefinition as a maturity concern, but I now think it is better treated as a pending application, because the performance is already confirmed across national laboratories. On the second point I would be slightly more cautious than you. The B014 theory credit is open, but the B005 credit is also not free of outside claims, namely other lattice-clock groups and ultrastable-laser developers, and I would not say the clock credit is uncontested, only that the contested parts lie outside the credited pair. I also note your recusal position on B046 and agree that it should not be advanced from this room; none of the preferred or alternative parts I propose touches that.

uncertainties: Fine priority between Katori's Tokyo group and Ye's Boulder group on the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice spectroscopy rests on recollection and has not been verified from the supplied material.

Whether the committee judges the lattice clock distinct enough from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize; I think the magic-wavelength idea makes it so, but I have not tested this against the exact prize citations.
How much of the 1e-18 result belongs to ultrastable-laser developers and ion-clock groups outside the credited pair.

Whether the committee prefers a measurement-science invention with tight credit (B005) over a younger new-phenomenon discovery with an unsettled mechanism and a harder credit problem (B014), which is a value judgment and not a factual question.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B005 or B014: none of Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer is among my documented connections. For B035, my PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+ and XL-Calibur collaborations and KTH astroparticle group are in an adjacent field, with no documented IceCube tie; I keep B035 only as an alternative and flag the proximity so colleagues can weigh my earlier first-place ranking of it accordingly. Unchanged from round 1.
